knownFor: French exile and author of the Institutes, who was held at Geneva in 1536 by William Farel's curse, was voted out in 1538 and came back in 1541 to give the city a written order for its church, with pastors, teachers, deacons and elders; the French and Scottish churches took up the same offices, and his name became the label for the family of Reformed churches.
datesNote: Born at Noyon in Picardy on 10 July 1509, as B. J. Kidd's note gives it; Beza's history of 1580 says only that he was a native of Noyon. He died on 27 May 1564. He was held at Geneva in August 1536, voted out in April 1538, called back by the city's councils in October 1540, and back in Geneva in September 1541. The preface that tells the scene at Geneva was written in 1557, about twenty-one years later. The Institutes dedication is dated 1 August 1536 in the 1559 text; the first edition's letter was dated 23 August 1535 and the book was printed in March 1536, as Kidd's and Beveridge's notes give it
role: Pastor and Bible lecturer at Geneva; author of the Institutes; drafter, with his colleagues, of the Church Ordinances of 1541

keyWorks.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
keyWorks.about: begun at Basel as a short handbook addressed to the French king, to clear the name of the believers burned in France; it grew from six chapters in 1536 to seventeen in 1539 and into the large work of 1559, in which he teaches that God chooses beforehand who will be saved

keyWorks.title: Church Ordinances of Geneva, 1541
keyWorks.about: the city's written rules for its church, drafted by Calvin and his colleagues with six councillors; they set four kinds of office, pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, and a weekly meeting of elders and pastors; the councils amended the draft, kept the last word on punishment, and the General Council passed it on 20 November 1541

keyWorks.title: Geneva Catechism
keyWorks.about: a book of questions and answers on the faith, which he says he wrote in haste on his return from Strasbourg, after the city swore to keep a catechism and a discipline; it opens by asking what is the chief end of man

traces: In September 1555 believers meeting in a Paris house chose a minister and set up a consistory of elders and deacons. The church history of 1580 says this followed the example of the early church; its modern editors tie it to the order Calvin gave the church at Strasbourg.

On 26 May 1559, with going to Geneva a crime that could cost a man his life under the edict of 1557, deputies of the French churches met secretly at Paris and wrote a statement of belief and a church discipline. B. J. Kidd counts ministers asked or sent from Geneva at nineteen in 1559, twelve in 1560 and ninety in 1561.

In December 1562 the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland ordered one uniform way of giving the sacraments and of marrying and burying, according to the church of Geneva. John Knox, by his own history, went to Frankfurt at Calvin's command, came back to Geneva and then went on to Scotland.
The Edinburgh Book of Common Order of 1611 still prints the catechism that Calvin made.

His name became the label for the whole family of churches: in 1672 a synod of the Greek church at Jerusalem met against the Calvinists, and a Dutch teacher at Utrecht, in lessons printed in 1662, said his church held with Calvin but he was not its head.
On 5 June 1559 Geneva opened its Academy, with Theodore Beza named Rector; B. J. Kidd reckons its students at twelve hundred junior and three hundred senior by 1564.
remembered: The church history of 1580 under Beza's name calls the Institutes an incomparable book.

Richard Hooker, writing against those who wanted Geneva's discipline in England, said about thirty years after Calvin's death that his books were almost the standard for judging doctrine and discipline, and that the French churches and the church of Scotland were cast in the mould Calvin had made.

uncertain: The scene at Geneva in 1536 rests on Calvin's own account in the preface to his Psalms commentary, written in 1557. His letter of 13 October 1536 says only that he was detained at Geneva by the brethren until they drew from him a promise to return. Calvin says war had closed the direct road to Strasbourg and that he meant to stay one night; Bonnet's note says he was going back to Basel by way of Geneva. The brief follows Calvin.

His conversion. He calls it a sudden conversion. B. J. Kidd, following Williston Walker, dates it late in 1532 or early in 1533, and writes that how far it took him toward his later teaching was perhaps as doubtful to Calvin as to us.

The Church Ordinances of 1541. The text in the Geneva archive is a draft with additions in another hand and a few words in Calvin's own; the official text differs from it. The councils amended it and would not let the ministers see the changes. The official text adds that the ministers have no civil jurisdiction and must report to the council wherever punishment is needed.

The quarrel with Bolsec rests on the Company of Pastors' own register, the city's sentence and a letter of Beza to Bullinger, which is the record of Geneva's side. Bern's pastors replied that some said Bolsec was not so bad a man. Calvin's 1552 treatise calls him a wandering vagabond sent by Satan. B. J. Kidd's summary of how the dispute fared with other churches is an editor's, and the council vote of November 1552 is not held as a primary line. Sebastian Castellio's writings against predestination are not held.
The Latin of the 1559 Institutes is not held. The teaching on predestination is rendered from Beveridge's English of 1845.

The death of Servetus. The sentence names books against the Trinity and against the baptism of infants. Calvin wrote in 1546 that if Servetus came he would not let him leave alive, and in August 1553 that he hoped for a death sentence but wished the punishment made less severe. The city council had first asked the advice of the churches of Bern, Basel, Zurich and Schaffhausen.

Who wrote the French statement of belief of 1559. Philip Schaff says it was prepared by Calvin and his pupil De Chandieu; B. J. Kidd says it was not Calvin's but the work of Antoine de la Roche Chandieu.
Whether the Paris congregation copied Geneva. The church history of 1580 names the early church as its model; its editors name Calvin's order at Strasbourg.

The farewell of 28 April 1564 is a minister's record. Pinant wrote it down as nearly as memory could keep it, and a second account confirms it. Kidd's French has fifty or sixty gunshots; Bonnet's English has forty or fifty.

Verdicts by B. J. Kidd that Library notes carry as the editor's, not as sources: that the Ordinances powerfully influenced all but Lutheran Protestantism, that after 1555 Calvin's party proceeded by banishment and executions against its opponents, and that the Academy made Geneva the intellectual and missionary center of the Reformed. Hooker's judgment of Calvin comes from a critic of the discipline, written about thirty years after his death.

briefReferences: Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms (1557), in B. J. Kidd's Latin: Farel holds him at Geneva by a curse; he had meant to stay one night on his way to Strasbourg; written about twenty-one years after the scene.

Preface to the Commentary on the Psalms; Institutes dedication to Francis I, tr. Henry Beveridge: born in France, he left it to hide in a quiet corner; at Basel believers burned in France were slandered as rebels; he wrote a short handbook to clear their name.
Council registers of 21 to 23 April 1538: Farel and Calvin banned from preaching, voted out of Geneva by the General Council.
Calvin's letters to Farel, tr. Jules Bonnet: from Strasbourg in 1540 he would rather die a hundred times than return; in 1541 he remembers he is not his own.
Council register of 13 September 1541 and the farewell of 1564: he would take his post only once the city swore to keep a catechism and a discipline.

Church Ordinances of 1541, draft in Calvini Opera X: four kinds of office; pastors; teachers; deacons for the poor and the sick; twelve elders from the city's councils; the weekly meeting with the pastors; the councils keep the last word on punishment. The General Council passes the text on 20 November 1541.
Registers of 1543 and 1555, in Kidd: the dispute over who could bar people from communion; the right confirmed in January 1555.
Gruet sentence of 1547, in Kidd: put to death for speaking against God, for acts against the government, and for threatening the pastors.
Institutes III.21.5 (1559), tr. Beveridge: God chooses beforehand who will be saved.

Register of the Company of Pastors, 16 October 1551; Bern's pastors' reply of 7 December 1551; the city's sentence of December 1551, in Kidd: Bolsec at the weekly Bible meeting, jailed, then banished.

Calvin's letters, 1546 and 1553, tr. Jules Bonnet; the sentence of 27 October 1553 in Calvini Opera VIII; the pastors' register of 27 October 1553: Servetus burned alive after the advice of four Swiss churches.
Histoire ecclésiastique of 1580 and Kidd's Nos. 324 to 327: the Paris congregation of 1555, the edict of 1557 and the secret national assembly of 1559.
General Assembly of December 1562, in the Book of the Universal Kirk: the order of the church of Geneva for the sacraments, marriages and burials.
Farewell to the ministers, 28 April 1564, in Kidd's French, taken down by Pinant: the gunshots and the timid scholar; death on 27 May 1564.
World census, the Reformed cities of Zurich and Geneva: his tradition, begun at Zurich before him.

quotationOriginals.modern: When he saw that asking got him nowhere, he went as far as a curse. He called on God to curse my quiet life if I held back from helping in so great a need. Struck by that terror, I gave up the journey I had begun.
quotationOriginals.printed: ubi se vidit rogando nihil proficere, usque ad exsecrationem descendit, ut Deus otio meo malediceret, si me a ferendis subsidiis in tanta necessitate subducerem. Quo terrore perculsus, susceptum iter ita omisi
quotationOriginals.work: Calvin, preface to the Commentary on the Psalms (1557), in B. J. Kidd, Documents Illustrative of the Continental Reformation

quotationOriginals.modern: I have lived here amid extraordinary battles. In mockery, I was greeted in the evening outside my door with fifty or sixty gunshots. Think how that could shake a poor, timid scholar, as I am and always have been, I confess.
quotationOriginals.printed: J'ay vescu icy en combats merveilleux : j'ay esté salué par mocquerie le soir devant ma porte de 50 ou 60 coups d'arquebute. Que pensez-vous que cela pouvoit estonner un pauvre escholier timide comme je suis, et comme je l'ay tousjours esté, je le confesse ?
quotationOriginals.work: Calvin's farewell to the ministers of Geneva, 28 April 1564, as taken down by the minister Pinant, in B. J. Kidd, Documents Illustrative of the Continental Reformation
